title: The Road to Palibothra: Megasthenes, the Indika, and the Country at the Edge of the Map
years: c. 350 BCE - c. 290 BCE (both dates modern convention, neither attested)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ionia, a birthplace no one writes down
stops.date_confidence: Modern handbook convention only. No ancient testimonium supplies Megasthenes with a birthplace, a family, or a birth year; the c. 350 BCE date and the Ionian origin are conveniences of the reference works, and the Smyrna coordinate stands in for 'Ionia', not for a documented city.
stops.campa: A Greek is born somewhere on the Ionian coast, in the generation that will watch Macedon swallow Persia. No source names his parents or his city, and the year is nobody's record. What the world keeps of him is four books about a country he has not yet heard of, and it keeps them only in fragments, quoted by men who mostly do not believe him. He is raised on a Greek in which India already exists as rumor: Herodotus on the ants that dig up gold, Ctesias on the men with dogs' heads. He will go and look, and come back saying the ants are real.
suggested_refs: The Ionian coast around Smyrna, conventional but undocumented placement of his origin
sources: A. B. Bosworth, 'The Historical Setting of Megasthenes' Indica', Classical Philology 91.2 (1996), 113-127
Wikipedia, 'Megasthenes' (checked 2026-08-27), which records the c. 350 birth date with no ancient support

stops.name: Old Kandahar, the house of Sibyrtius
stops.date_confidence: The association with Sibyrtius is attested, in a single clause of Arrian, Anabasis 5.6.2. The year is inferred from Sibyrtius' appointment to Arachosia and Gedrosia early in 324 BCE; Arrian gives neither Megasthenes' rank nor the length of his stay. Identifying the satrapal seat with Old Kandahar is the standard modern siting of Alexandria in Arachosia, not an ancient statement.
stops.campa: Sibyrtius takes the satrapy of Arachosia and Gedrosia, and in his household at the Alexander-city under the Kandahar rock there is a Greek named Megasthenes. The roads from Persia, from Bactria and from the Indus meet here, and the Ganges is talked about in the streets as a river with traffic on it rather than as a story. Arrian will record the arrangement in one clause and nothing more: he lived with Sibyrtius. The clause gives no rank, no office, no length of stay, and no account of how he came to be there in the first place.
stops.quote: lived with Sibyrtius, satrap of Arachosia, and says that he often visited Sandracottus, king of the Indians
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 5.6.2, as translated in J. W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian (1877)
suggested_refs: The citadel mound of Old Kandahar, identified with Alexandria in Arachosia; excavated in the 1970s and again in 2008-2009 without a confirmed Greek building

stops.name: Old Kandahar, the news from Babylon
stops.date_confidence: Alexander's death at Babylon in June 323 BCE is secure. Megasthenes' presence in Arachosia at that moment is inference from his documented association with Sibyrtius, not attestation; no source places him anywhere in these years.
stops.campa: Alexander dies at Babylon and the empire he has not finished conquering is cut up among his generals within the month. In Arachosia the news arrives late, along the same roads the elephants came down. Eastward the Macedonian garrisons in the Punjab begin to thin, and a young king the Greeks will call Sandracottus takes country nobody in Kandahar can defend. The Greek in the satrap's household keeps whatever place he holds in it: Sibyrtius is left in Arachosia at the settlement of Babylon in 323, and left there again at Triparadeisus in 321.
suggested_refs: The Successor settlements of Babylon (323) and Triparadeisus (321), which left Sibyrtius in place
sources: Standard Successor chronology as summarized in Bosworth 1996

stops.name: Old Kandahar, confirmed a third time
stops.date_confidence: Attested for Sibyrtius: after defeating Eumenes, Antigonus confirmed him in Arachosia and reinforced him with a contingent of the Silver Shields. Nothing attests Megasthenes there in that year; the stop marks the continuity of the household he is documented as belonging to.
stops.campa: Antigonus breaks Eumenes in Iran and, dealing out the east again, confirms Arachosia to Sibyrtius for the third time in seven years. With the confirmation come the Silver Shields, the veteran infantry no commander wants standing near him, sent east to be used up. Kandahar is quiet in a way the rest of the empire is not, a place where a Greek can sit still while the Successors ruin one another further west. It is the last western post on the road that runs down to the Ganges, and the road is open.
suggested_refs: The Silver Shields, dispersed eastward into Arachosia by Antigonus after 316 BCE

stops.name: Old Kandahar, sent down the Indus road
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the central chronological dispute of the subject. Bosworth (1996) argues for a mission out of Arachosia c. 320-318 BCE; the conventional handbook account instead makes Megasthenes' first journey a Seleucid embassy after the settlement of 305 BCE. No ancient source dates any journey of his. The two datings are carried here side by side and not reconciled.
stops.campa: He goes east. The mission is Sibyrtius's, and the road runs down through the passes to the Indus and then out across the Punjab, through kingdoms Alexander took eight years ago and no Macedonian now holds. Arrian's word for what follows is that he visited Sandracottus often, which describes a habit rather than a single embassy. Everything else, the year of the journey, its size and its purpose, is reconstruction laid over that one clause. Whether he carries letters, gifts, or only instructions to look, no source says.
suggested_refs: The Arachosia-to-Punjab road, the only land route between Sibyrtius' seat and the Gangetic plain
sources: Strabo, Geography 2.1.9 and 15.1.36 for the conventional Seleucid embassy

stops.name: The Indus at Ohind, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: Route inference only. No ancient text places Megasthenes at this or any crossing; the ford below Ohind is the standard passage used by Alexander's army and by later traffic between the Iranian plateau and the Punjab, and is included as the obligatory point on any plausible road east.
stops.campa: The river is crossed below Ohind, at the ford Alexander's engineers once bridged with boats, where the water spreads wide and slow before the Punjab begins. No source puts Megasthenes on this bank or any other. The road east simply passes here, as every army and every embassy between the plateau and India has passed here. The Indus is the first of the fifty-eight navigable rivers his book will count, and the only great one whose mouth he never sees.
suggested_refs: The Indus ford at Ohind (Hund), crossing point of Alexander's army in 327 BCE
sources: Route reconstruction from Arrian's Anabasis geography
Arrian, Indika, for the count of fifty-eight navigable rivers

stops.name: Taxila, the city of the naked philosophers
stops.date_confidence: Inference, not attestation: no fragment names Megasthenes at Taxila. Coordinate inherited unchanged from alexander.journey.json, whose Taxila stop marks the same city in 326 BCE.
stops.campa: Taxila stands on the Bhir Mound, a trading city of the Gandharan plain that opened its gates to Alexander without a fight and whose naked philosophers argued with his officers, sitting in the sun and refusing to stand up for anybody. Whether Megasthenes passes through, no text says; the road east goes nowhere else. The ascetics of the Punjab are the first Greek version of a subject he will give a long stretch of his own book to: who in India thinks for a living, what they eat, whether they marry, what they say about dying.
suggested_refs: The Bhir Mound at Taxila, the city level standing in the late fourth century BCE
sources: alexander.journey.json, stop 'Taxila, the riddles of the naked philosophers'
Arrian, Indika, on the Greek encounter with the gymnosophists via Onesicritus
Strabo, Geography 15.1.59-60, for Megasthenes on the Brachmanes and Garmanes

stops.name: The Hydaspes, Porus still alive
stops.date_confidence: Contested, and flagged rather than settled. The received manuscript text of Arrian, Indika 5.3 has Megasthenes say he met both Sandracottus and Porus. Editors have emended or deleted the clause since the eighteenth century, because on the conventional post-305 dating Porus is long dead; Diodorus 19.14.8 has Eudamus obtain his elephants by assassinating Porus, and the killing is placed variously between 321 and 315 BCE, commonly c. 318. Bosworth (1996) defends the manuscript and dates the meeting to this window. The coordinate is inherited from alexander.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the Hydaspes, where Alexander broke Porus in the rain and then handed him back his kingdom enlarged, Megasthenes says he met the king himself. Editors have deleted the sentence, emended it, and explained it away for two centuries, on the ground that Porus is a decade dead before Megasthenes ever comes east. Bosworth keeps the sentence and moves the man instead, to a mission out of Arachosia around 319, when Porus is alive and still ruling the country between the rivers that Alexander gave back to him.
stops.quote: Sandracottus, the greatest of the Indian kings, and Porus, even greater than he was
stops.quote_source: Arrian, Indika 5.3, received manuscript text, Fordham translation
suggested_refs: The Hydaspes battlefield near Jhelum, where Porus was defeated and restored in 326 BCE
sources: Diodorus Siculus 19.14.8 on Eudamus and the death of Porus

stops.name: The Hyphasis, the limit the Macedonians would not cross
stops.date_confidence: The mutiny at the Hyphasis in 326 BCE belongs to Alexander, not to Megasthenes. Arrian's comparative judgment on how much of India Megasthenes saw is attested; that Megasthenes crossed at this exact point is inference. Coordinate inherited from alexander.journey.json.
stops.campa: At the Beas the Macedonian army stopped, seven years back, and refused to go further; Alexander sacrificed for a crossing, got bad omens, and turned around. Megasthenes crosses. Beyond lies the country no Greek under arms has entered, and he goes into it as a guest and not a soldier, which is why the book he brings back can describe a kingdom instead of a campaign. Arrian, reading him four centuries on, weighs what he saw and finds it modest. Behind him on the west bank stand twelve altars raised to twelve gods.
stops.quote: But not even Megasthenes, so far as I can see, travelled over any large part of India; yet a good deal more than the followers of Alexander son of Philip did.
suggested_refs: The twelve altars raised on the Hyphasis at the eastern limit of the Macedonian march

stops.name: Mathura, down the Yamuna
stops.date_confidence: Route inference; no ancient text names Megasthenes on the Yamuna corridor. Included as an obligatory waypoint on the reconstructed itinerary between the Punjab and the Ganges.
stops.campa: The road bends southeast off the Punjab plain and follows the Yamuna down through Mathura, a city of the Surasena on the river's west bank, whose kings the Greek reports say worship a Heracles of their own. From here the two great rivers run toward each other for hundreds of miles. What the surviving fragments have is a river system set out from the inside, tributary by tributary, at a level of detail nobody assembles from hearsay in Kandahar. Nothing in them puts Megasthenes on this stretch by name.
suggested_refs: The Yamuna corridor through Mathura, land route between the Punjab and the Gangetic plain
sources: Arrian, Indika 4, on the Indian rivers

stops.name: Prayaga, where the two rivers meet
stops.date_confidence: The river measurements are attested to Megasthenes by name in Strabo 15.1.35. His personal presence at the confluence is inference from the itinerary, not attestation.
stops.campa: The Yamuna comes in from the west and the Ganges from the north, and below the junction the water runs a hundred stadia wide in an ordinary season, twenty fathoms at its shallowest. Megasthenes measures, or is given measurements, and puts numbers into his book where Herodotus put wonder. A hundred stadia is a figure a man can be given by a boatman or can pace out on a bank, and the fragments do not say which he did. Eratosthenes will take India's whole length from him, sixteen thousand stadia, and Strabo records the two of them agreeing on that figure at 15.1.11.
stops.quote: Megasthenes says that when its breadth is medium it widens even to one hundred stadia and that its least depth is twenty fathoms
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.35 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: The Ganges-Yamuna confluence at Prayaga, geographic hinge of the Megasthenic river catalogue
sources: strabo.journey.json, stop 'Amaseia, Megasthenes beyond all bounds'

stops.name: The Erannoboas, arrival at the confluence
stops.date_confidence: That Megasthenes reached Chandragupta's capital is attested (Strabo 15.1.36; Arrian, Anabasis 5.6.2). The year is the disputed embassy window. The equation of the Erannoboas with the Son is the standard modern identification, not a statement of Arrian's.
stops.campa: Where the Son comes into the Ganges the greatest city in India stands on the tongue of land between the two waters, and the Greeks write its name Palibothra. Megasthenes arrives in the reign of Chandragupta Maurya, whose name their tongues make Sandracottus, some twenty years after the Nanda kings were pulled down. He will describe it well enough that men digging in Patna twenty-two centuries later will know what they have found. The city is timber throughout: wall of wood, towers of wood, the king's hall of wood, cut out of forests upriver and floated down to it.
stops.quote: the greatest of the Indian cities is called Palimbothra... at the confluence of the Erannoboas and the Ganges
suggested_refs: The confluence of the Son and the Ganges below Patna, site of the Mauryan capital

stops.name: Bulandi Bagh, the wall of eighty stadia
stops.date_confidence: The description is securely Megasthenic: Strabo 15.1.36 for the eighty by fifteen stadia, the parallelogram, the perforated timber wall and the ditch that doubles as a sewer, with Megasthenes named at 15.1.35-37; Arrian, Indika 10 adds 570 towers, 64 gates, and a ditch six plethra wide and thirty cubits deep. The date is the disputed window. The coordinate is the Bulandi Bagh palisade site, roughly 350 m north of the Kumhrar hall and distinct from it; the ancient city's full extent is not fixed.
stops.campa: He paces the wall, or is walked along it: eighty stadia by fifteen, a parallelogram of timber pierced with holes so archers can shoot through it, and in front of the wall a ditch that carries both the assault and the sewage of the city. Arrian's version of the same account counts five hundred and seventy towers and sixty-four gates, and gives the ditch six plethra of width and thirty cubits of depth. No Greek describes an Indian city in this much measured detail again. Waddell put a spade into the ground at Bulandi Bagh in 1895 and found the palisade where the numbers said it would be.
stops.quote: It is said that Palibothra lies at the confluence of the Ganges and the other river, a city eighty stadia in length and fifteen in breadth, in the shape of a parallelogram, and surrounded by a wooden wall that is perforated so that arrows can be shot through the holes; and that in front of the wall lies a trench used both for defence and as a receptacle of the sewage that flows from the city
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.36 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: The timber palisade of Pataliputra at Bulandi Bagh, uncovered by L. A. Waddell in 1895 and since traced over several kilometres
sources: Wikipedia, 'Pataliputra' and 'Kumhrar', on the Waddell excavation of 1895

stops.name: Kumhrar, the hall of eighty pillars
stops.date_confidence: That Megasthenes described the Mauryan court is attested through Strabo, Geography 15.1. The physical correlation with the Kumhrar excavations is a modern archaeological inference and no ancient text connects the two: Spooner dug the site in 1912-13 and Jaiswal in 1951-55, recovering one whole monolith and the pits of seventy-nine more.
stops.campa: Inside the wall stands the king's hall, its roof carried on eighty pillars of polished sandstone set in eight rows of ten, each monolith taller than five men and buffed until it holds a reflection. Megasthenes gives a fortified royal residence, processions under guard, and court ceremony elaborate enough that a Greek thinks it worth setting down at length. What he watched and what he was told he does not separate, and no fragment says whether he had an interpreter or how much of the language he had.
suggested_refs: The eighty-pillared Mauryan hall at Kumhrar, 5 km east of Patna railway station, its monoliths of black-spotted buff sandstone standing 9.75 m
sources: Strabo, Geography 15.1 on the Megasthenic court material
Wikipedia, 'Kumhrar' (D. B. Spooner 1912-13; K. P. Jaiswal 1951-55)

stops.name: Palibothra, the seven divisions
stops.date_confidence: The report is securely Megasthenic, preserved in Arrian's Indika. Its accuracy is a separate question: modern scholarship, Bosworth included, generally reads the sevenfold scheme as a Greek analytical grid laid over Indian social and occupational reality rather than a transparent rendering of varna. Attested as his claim, not as fact.
stops.campa: He sorts India into seven kinds of people: wise men, farmers, herdsmen, artisans and traders, soldiers, overseers, and the councillors who deliberate with the king. Nobody may marry outside his own kind or take up another kind's work. It is a clean scheme, sevenfold like the Egyptian classes Herodotus counted, and it matches no order that Indian sources describe. Whether he was handed it, inferred it, or built it out of a Greek habit of dividing foreigners into sevens, the fragments do not say.
suggested_refs: Arrian, Indika 11-12, the fullest surviving statement of the sevenfold division
sources: Arrian, Indika (sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu): 'The Indians generally are divided into seven castes'

stops.name: Palibothra, the Brachmanes and the Sarmanes
stops.date_confidence: Attested to Megasthenes by multiple independent later authors (Strabo 15.1.59-60; Clement, Stromateis 1.15). Whether he observed the philosophers himself or worked from informants and interpreters is established by no source.
stops.campa: Of the first division he makes two kinds. The Brachmanes live in the cities and about the king, are consulted at the year's turning on drought and disease and the weather, and are sparing with words. The Garmanes, whom one branch calls the Hylobii, live in the forests on leaves and wild fruit, clothe themselves in bark, take no wives, and are asked about death. Clement of Alexandria, five centuries later, will read this page and set the Brahmins beside the Jews as the two peoples outside Greece who said what the Greeks said about nature.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 15.1.59-60, the Brachmanes and Garmanes passage

stops.name: Palibothra, tables of gold and boiled rice
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and unusually well anchored: Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 4.153, cites the second book of the Indika by number. It is one of only a handful of fragments tied to a numbered book, Clement's citation of the third book being the other.
stops.campa: At table each man is served alone, at a board set for him, and a golden dish is put in front of him. Boiled rice goes into it first, handled the way a Greek handles barley groats, and then the meats, dressed in the Indian manner. The detail is of no use to a geographer or a general, and it is the kind of thing a man writes down when he has sat at the meal himself, though no source says he did. Athenaeus quotes the passage out of the second book of the Indika, which makes it one of the few fragments that says which book it came from.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophists 4.153, citing the second book of the Indika by number
sources: Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis 1.15, citing the third book

stops.name: The royal camp, forty thousand and no thieves
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Strabo, Geography 15.1.53, reports the anecdote as Megasthenes' own testimony from inside the camp. The camp is itinerant and no source gives it a site, so the coordinate marks the Pataliputra region generally.
stops.campa: The king moves and the country moves with him: a camp of forty thousand people pitched on the plain, tents and animals and traders and the whole apparatus of a court that governs from wherever it is standing. Megasthenes lives in it. On no single day of his time there, he says, did the thefts reported come to more than two hundred drachmae, and this among a people who keep no written laws. The figure of forty thousand is his own; an older English rendering multiplied it by ten, and the four hundred thousand is still in circulation.
suggested_refs: The itinerant Mauryan royal camp, described from the inside at Strabo 15.1.53
sources: Strabo, Geography 15.1.53 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius): 'although the number in camp was forty thousand'
Older Bohn/Hamilton-Falconer rendering, source of the inflated 400,000 figure

segments.name: The Country as He Sets It Down

stops.name: The elephant forests of the Gangetic east
stops.date_confidence: The elephant material is attested to Megasthenes in Strabo, Geography 15.1. No ancient source locates the capture grounds; the coordinate is an approximate regional placeholder in the humid east that Thomas Trautmann identifies as the elephant-supplying zone, as distinct from the horse-supplying northwest.
stops.campa: East of the capital the forests begin, and in them the king's men dig pits, drive wild elephants in behind tame decoys, starve them quiet, and bring them out broken to work. Megasthenes writes down the capture, the taming, the medicine given for their sicknesses, and the rule that the animals belong to the king and to nobody else. The dry northwest supplies horses and the wet east supplies elephants; the empire is built on the difference. Five hundred of the eastern beasts go west to Seleucus in the settlement of 305.
suggested_refs: The elephant-capture grounds of the Gangetic borderlands, the military-livestock base of Mauryan power
sources: Thomas Trautmann, 'Megasthenes on the Military Livestock of Chandragupta', Comparative Studies in Society and History 63.2 (2021), 339-365

stops.name: Among the Prasii, the largest tigers in India
stops.date_confidence: Attested to Megasthenes at Strabo, Geography 15.1.37. No ancient location is given for the animals beyond 'among the Prasii', the eastern people of the Gangetic plain; the coordinate is an approximate regional placeholder east of Pataliputra.
stops.campa: Among the Prasii, the eastern people whose king Sandracottus is, Megasthenes reports the largest tigers in India, nearly twice the size of lions. Apes come next in the same passage, and after them the other animals of the country, each entered as flatly as the rivers were. The catalogue runs together what a man could see from a road and what was told to him by people who enjoyed the telling, and it does not mark which is which. Did he ever stand in front of one of these tigers? Strabo copies the passage out at 15.1.37 without asking, and no other source answers it.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 15.1.37, the Megasthenic catalogue of Indian animals
sources: Strabo, Geography 2.1.9, for the contrary verdict on his reliability

stops.name: The mouth of the Indus, fifty-eight rivers counted
stops.date_confidence: The figure of fifty-eight navigable rivers is Megasthenes' own claim, preserved verbatim by Arrian in the Indika. Nothing suggests he saw the delta; the coordinate at the Indus mouth is a representative pin for the river catalogue, not a stop on any reconstructed itinerary.
stops.campa: The Indus goes down through Sind in braided channels and empties into a sea Greeks have only lately sailed. Megasthenes counts fifty-eight navigable rivers in India and sets the Indus and the Ganges at the head of the list, the Ganges the greater of the two. He never sees this delta. Nearchus sailed it out of Alexander's fleet and the coast comes to Megasthenes on other men's word, which he takes and enters at the same weight as the things he measured himself. Which fifty-eight he meant has never been worked out.
suggested_refs: The Indus delta below Thatta, the coast Nearchus sailed and Megasthenes reported at second hand
sources: Arrian, Indika (Fordham): 'he states the number of Indian rivers in all to be fifty-eight, and these all navigable'

stops.name: Palibothra, no Indian uses slaves
stops.date_confidence: Attested as his claim and flagged as contradicted in the ancient record itself: Strabo, Geography 15.1.54 sets it directly against Onesicritus, who says the opposite and names a place. Strabo prints both and adjudicates neither, and neither does this file.
stops.campa: No Indian, he writes, uses slaves. In a country he has crossed on foot, in a camp of forty thousand, at a court whose divisions of society he counted one by one, he reports that not one person there is owned. Onesicritus, who came east with Alexander's fleet and got as far as the lower Indus, says the opposite and gives it an address: slavery is peculiar to the Indians in the country of Musicanus. Strabo sets the two statements side by side in a single sentence and chooses neither.
stops.quote: although Megasthenes says that no Indian uses slaves, Onesicritus declares that slavery is peculiar to the Indians in the country of Musicanus
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.54 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 15.1.54, where the two Greek reports on Indian slavery stand unreconciled

stops.name: Mount Meros, where Dionysus stopped
stops.date_confidence: Content of the Indika, not a documented stop: no source places Megasthenes at Nysa, and the date orders the segment only. The material itself is attested, but split between two authors. Diodorus 2.38-39 supplies the heat, the withdrawal into the hills, the cities, the laws, the wine and the fifty-two years; Arrian, Indika 7-8 supplies the thigh-etymology of Meros and the reigns. The siting of Nysa near Jalalabad is a traditional modern identification and is contested.
stops.campa: Above the Kabul road a mountain stands over a town the Greeks call Nysa, and they name the mountain Meros, thigh, after the place Dionysus was carried before he was born. The god came into India with an army, Megasthenes reports, lost men to heat and a wasting sickness on the plain, took them up into the hills to recover, founded cities there, taught the vine and the plough, gave laws and set up courts, and ruled fifty-two years before dying old. Diodorus keeps the fifty-two years. Arrian keeps the etymology of the thigh.
suggested_refs: The mountain traditionally identified as Meros above Nysa, near Jalalabad, an identification contested among scholars
sources: J. W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian (1877)

stops.name: The kingdom of Pandaea in the south
stops.date_confidence: Content of the Indika, reported through Arrian and Pliny; no source places Megasthenes anywhere in southern India, and the date orders the segment only. The equation of the legendary Pandaea with the historical Pandya kingdom is a long-standing medieval and modern identification that Arrian himself never makes.
stops.campa: South of everything, past the rivers, an Indian Heracles is said to have fathered many sons and one daughter, born to him late, whom he called Pandaea and to whom he gave the country of the far south: five hundred elephants, four thousand horse, a hundred and thirty thousand foot. The women there marry at seven and the men are old at forty. Later readers put Pandaea's country in the Tamil land of the Pandyas, an identification the fragments do not make and cannot support.
suggested_refs: The Pandya country around Madurai, traditionally identified with the Pandaea of the fragments
sources: Arrian, Indika (Fordham): 'he had only one daughter, called Pandaea'
Pliny, Natural History, Megasthenic material on the Indian Heracles

stops.name: Mount Nulus, the feet turned backwards
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a Megasthenic claim: Pliny names him in the sentence itself, Natural History 7.2.22. No securely identifiable location for Nulus survives; the coordinate is an approximate Himalayan placeholder consistent with the neighbouring marvel-peoples of the same passage. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: On the mountain called Nulus there are people whose feet point backwards, eight toes on each foot, walking away from the direction they are going. Nobody has found Nulus. It sits in a passage of Pliny alongside three or four other mountain peoples of India, some credited to Megasthenes and some to Ctesias, all of them set at the edge of the country where the roads run out and the reports arrive secondhand from men paid to bring them. Pliny names Megasthenes inside the sentence itself, at Natural History 7.2.22, and that is the whole reason the fragment survives.
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 7.2.22, the Nulus passage with its explicit Megasthenes attribution
sources: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 7.2.22 (Latin at LacusCurtius; English at attalus.org/pliny/hn7a.html)

stops.name: The mountains of the dog-headed men
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a claim Megasthenes made, by Pliny's explicit citation at Natural History 7.2.22-23. One correction to the usual quotation: the census clause counting more than 120,000 of them belongs, in Pliny's Latin, to Ctesias and not to Megasthenes, and is excluded here. No ancient source gives the mountains a location; the coordinate is an approximate placeholder in the Himalayan borderlands where such peoples were conventionally set.
stops.campa: On many of the mountains, Megasthenes writes, there is a race of men with the heads of dogs. They wear the skins of wild animals, they speak by barking, they live by hunting and fowling and use their nails for weapons. Pliny the Elder copies the passage into the seventh book of the Natural History under its author's name, and out of Pliny it goes into Solinus, and out of Solinus into every medieval account of the world's edges, until dog-headed men are standing in the margins of psalters four thousand miles from any mountain in India.
stops.quote: Megasthenes states that on the mountain named Nulus there are people with their feet turned backwards and with eight toes on each foot, while on many of the mountains there is a tribe of human beings with dogs' heads, who wear a covering of wild beasts' skins, whose speech is a bark and who live on the produce of hunting and fowling, for which they use their nails as weapons.
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 7.2.22-23 (Rackham, Loeb)
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 7.2.22-23, the cynocephali passage that carried the motif into Roman encyclopedism
sources: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 7.2.22-23 (attalus.org; Latin at penelope.uchicago.edu)
san_cristobal.journey.json (the cynocephali and the Ratramnus ruling)
saint_mercurius.journey.json; odoric_of_pordenone.journey.json, 'Nicoveran, the island of the dog-faced men'; ibn_battuta.journey.json, 'Barahnakar, the coast of the dog-mouthed men'

stops.name: Near the source of the Ganges, the Astomi
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a Megasthenic claim through Pliny, Natural History 7.2.25, with a parallel version at Strabo 15.1.57. Anatomically impossible as a literal population. No precise ancient coordinate survives; the pin sits at the traditional source of the Ganges, the conventional edge-of-world zone for such reports.
stops.campa: At the far eastern boundary of India, near the source of the Ganges, live the Astomi, who have no mouths. Their bodies are hairy all over, they clothe themselves in cotton down, and they live on what they breathe: the scent of roots, of flowers, of wild apples, which they carry with them on long journeys so as never to be without a supply. A strong smell kills them. Strabo carries a version of the report at 15.1.57 in which such people are brought in and shown to visitors, standing in a room where a Greek could look at them.
stops.quote: At the extreme boundary of India to the East, near the source of the Ganges, he puts the Astomi tribe, that has no mouth and a body hairy all over; they dress in cotton-wool and live only on the air they breathe and the scent they inhale through their nostrils
stops.quote_source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 7.2.25 (via attalus.org)
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 7.2.25; Strabo, Geography 15.1.57, the parallel Astomi report
sources: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)

stops.name: India, the ears that reach the feet
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a Megasthenic claim by Strabo, Geography 15.1.57, in the catalogue he assembles in order to attack it. No location is given in any source; the coordinate is an approximate Himalayan placeholder, and the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: There are men whose ears come down to their feet, and who sleep in them. They are strong enough to pull up trees with their hands and to snap a bowstring. Megasthenes puts them in the Indika together with people five spans tall, people three spans tall, and people with no nostrils who breathe through two holes above the mouth. He is not the first Greek to report any of it. Ctesias, physician at the Persian court, had most of them a century earlier without going east of Susa, and Megasthenes, who has been to India, sets them down again. Strabo prints the whole list at 15.1.57 in order to attack it.
stops.quote: Enotocoetae, who have ears that extend to their feet, so that they can sleep in them, and are strong enough to pluck up trees and to break bowstrings
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57, the catalogue of fabulous peoples attributed to Megasthenes
sources: Strabo, Geography 2.1.9, the parallel list in the attack on the writers on India

stops.name: The country of the pygmies and the cranes
stops.date_confidence: Attested as Strabo's charge against him at Geography 2.1.9 and 15.1.57. No ancient coordinate survives; the pin is a placeholder at the conventional eastern fringe. Strabo's own practice contradicts his verdict, and the contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The pygmies are three spans tall and the cranes come down to make war on them every year, as they do in the second book of the Iliad. Megasthenes takes the oldest Greek story about the edge of the world and sets it inside a report on a real embassy to a real king. Strabo, who quotes his measurements of the Ganges with respect, uses this to rank the writers on India as fabricators and puts him second worst, after Deimachus. Both verdicts stand in the same work, thirteen books apart.
stops.quote: Megasthenes, going beyond all bounds to the realm of myth, speaks of people five spans long and three spans long, some without nostrils, having instead merely two breathing orifices above their mouths
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 2.1.9, the ranking of Deimachus first and Megasthenes second among fabricators
sources: strabo.journey.json, stop 'Amaseia, Megasthenes beyond all bounds'

stops.name: The Derdae, and the ants that dig gold
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim to Megasthenes at Strabo, Geography 15.1.44. The geography is a problem the pin cannot hide: Strabo's own text puts the Derdae 'towards the east and in the mountains', while the coordinate used here is Gilgit, in the far northwest, chosen on the Dardistan etymology. The two do not agree, and the disagreement is left open rather than papered over.
stops.campa: Among the Derdae, where a plateau runs three thousand stadia around, there are ants the size of foxes that dig gold-bearing earth and heap it at their burrow mouths like moles. The people of the country steal the heaps while the ants are busy with pieces of wild-beast flesh thrown out to distract them. Herodotus told the story first. Megasthenes gives it a tribe and a place, which is what turns a wonder into a report, and the place he gives it does not fit the direction he gives it.
stops.quote: Megasthenes speaks of these ants as follows: that among the Derdae, a large tribe of Indians living towards the east and in the mountains, there is a plateau approximately three thousand stadia in circuit, and that below it are gold mines, of which the miners are ants, animals that are no smaller than foxes, are surpassingly swift, and live on the prey they catch.
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.44 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: The historical Dardistan around Gilgit, the conventional modern siting of the Derdae, contradicting Strabo's own 'towards the east'
sources: Herodotus 3.102-105, the earlier version of the gold-digging ants

stops.name: Taprobane, the island he never saw
stops.date_confidence: Attested as his claim by Pliny's explicit citation at Natural History 6.81. There is no evidence at all that Megasthenes visited the island; this is content of the book relayed by informants, and the date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Off the southern point of India lies an island the Greeks call Taprobane, and Megasthenes says a river cuts it in two, that its people are called the Palaeogoni, and that it yields more gold and bigger pearls than India itself. He has not been there. The island is reported to him, or read by him, and he enters it in his geography with the same flat confidence he gives the wall of Palibothra, which he paced himself. Taprobane will stay on Greek and Roman maps for centuries as the last land before the edge. Pliny keeps the sentence and the name at Natural History 6.81.
suggested_refs: Pliny, Natural History 6.81, the Megasthenic account of Taprobane

segments.name: Four Books, Written Before Seleucus Crossed

stops.name: Old Kandahar, the four books
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No source records where or when the Indika was composed. Bosworth argues from internal evidence for a date before Seleucus' Indian campaign, since the book claims Alexander alone invaded India in arms; the c. 310 date and the Arachosian setting are his, not an attested fact. The book numbers themselves are attested: Athenaeus 4.153 cites book 2, Clement, Stromateis 1.15 cites book 3.
stops.campa: The Indika runs to four books. Athenaeus quotes the second for the way food is served at the Mauryan court; Clement of Alexandria quotes the third for a sentence setting Brahmins and Jews together as the philosophers outside Greece who arrived at what the Greeks arrived at. Where it was written, and when, is recorded nowhere. Bosworth argues it from inside the text: the book states that Alexander alone came into India under arms, and no man writes that sentence after Seleucus has crossed the Indus in 305.
stops.quote: Very clearly the author Megasthenes... writes as follows in the third of his books, On Indian Affairs: All that was said about nature by the ancients is said also by those who philosophise beyond Greece: some things by the Brahmins among the Indians, and others by those called Jews in Syria.
suggested_refs: The four books of the Indika, lost entire and known only through quotation

stops.name: Old Kandahar, the country no army ever entered
stops.date_confidence: Attested as his claim in two independent branches: Strabo 15.1.6 for the denial that any outside army mastered India except Heracles, Dionysus and the Macedonians, and Arrian, Indika 5 for the named list of failed invaders, Sesostris, Idanthyrsus and Semiramis. The Persians appear in the Strabo branch, not in Arrian's sentence. The claim is contradicted by independent evidence of Achaemenid control in the Indus region; the contradiction is flagged and not resolved.
stops.campa: The claim runs through the whole book. No Indian army has ever gone abroad to conquer, and no foreign army has ever come in and mastered the country: not Sesostris out of Egypt, not Idanthyrsus the Scythian, not Semiramis, who died before she could make the attempt. Only Heracles and Dionysus, who were gods, and the Macedonians, who are recent. The Persians held the Indus valley for a century and a half before Alexander and took tribute out of it, and the book has nothing to say about them.
stops.quote: neither was an army ever sent outside the country by the Indians nor did any outside army ever invade their country and master them, except that with Heracles and Dionysus and that in our times with the Macedonians
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.6 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: Arrian, Indika 5, the list of invaders who failed where Alexander succeeded
sources: A. B. Bosworth, Classical Philology 91.2 (1996), on the political use of the claim

stops.name: Babylon, with Seleucus Nicator
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place, attestation as to the association. Clement, Stromateis 1.15, is the only ancient source stating that Megasthenes lived with Seleucus Nicator, and it gives neither place, date nor capacity. Babylon is Seleucus' principal early eastern seat; he founds Seleucia on the Tigris c. 305 and Antioch on the Orontes in 300, and no ancient text places Megasthenes at any of the three.
stops.campa: Clement, writing four and a half centuries later in Alexandria, says in one clause that Megasthenes the historian lived with Seleucus Nicator. It is the only ancient statement of the connection and it fixes nothing: not the place, not the years, not the capacity. No document naming both men has ever been found. Seleucus' eastern seat in this decade is Babylon; he founds Seleucia on the Tigris around 305 and Antioch on the Orontes in 300, moving his court twice while whatever this association was continued.
suggested_refs: The ruin field of Babylon, Seleucus' principal seat before the founding of Seleucia on the Tigris
sources: Clement of Alexandria, Stromateis 1.72 (Schwanbeck fragment 42), quoted in McCrindle 1877
Seleucid political geography; no ancient text places Megasthenes at Babylon

segments.name: The Embassy, and the Silence After It

stops.name: Palibothra, sent on embassy to Sandrocottus
stops.date_confidence: The embassy itself is attested: Strabo 15.1.36 names Megasthenes as the man sent to King Sandrocottus. The date is not. No ancient sentence dates the mission, and the c. 303-298 window is a modern handbook synthesis built on the Seleucid-Mauryan settlement of 305. Bosworth's alternative makes the earlier journey the real one and this a return; Arrian's 'often visited' is compatible with both. Unresolved.
stops.campa: Seleucus crosses the Indus, fights Chandragupta, and settles with him: the eastern provinces go to the Mauryan, a marriage of disputed meaning is agreed, and five hundred elephants come west. An envoy is then sent down to Palibothra, and Strabo names him in a single relative clause hung off a description of the city. This is the embassy the reference books mean when they date Megasthenes to 303: a man in his fifties going back over a road he has walked, to a king he already knows, for a new master. Nothing in Strabo dates it.
stops.quote: King Sandrocottus to whom Megasthenes was sent on an embassy
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.36 (Loeb, H. L. Jones, via LacusCurtius)
suggested_refs: The Seleucid-Mauryan settlement of 305 BCE and the five hundred elephants ceded to Seleucus

stops.name: An unrecorded place, the death nobody writes down
stops.date_confidence: Negative finding, stated as one. No ancient source records when, where or how Megasthenes died, and there is no tomb, epitaph, burial, coin, portrait, papyrus or inscription naming him. The c. 290 date is modern handbook convention counted forward from a birth date that is also convention. The coordinate reuses Palibothra only because it is the last place any source puts him alive, and is not a claim that he died there.
stops.campa: After the embassy the record stops. No source says where he went, what he did next, when he died or how. There is no tomb, no epitaph, no coin, no inscription, no portrait: nothing survives of him that is not a sentence inside another man's book. The date of about 290 BCE printed in the reference works is a convenience, counted forward from a birth date that is also a convenience. Palibothra, where he was sent on the embassy, is the last place any ancient source puts him alive.
suggested_refs: The absence of any monument, inscription or portrait: the whole of the physical record
sources: Wikipedia, 'Megasthenes' (checked 2026-08-27), which records only 'died c. 290 BCE'
Negative finding across Arrian, Strabo, Clement, Pliny and Athenaeus, none of which records a death

stops.name: Palibothra, a book kept alive by men who disbelieve it
stops.date_confidence: Transmission history, attested by the surviving citations themselves. The date is nominal, placed at the close of the subject's own life to order the segment; the quoters and editors named here belong to their own centuries and their own files. Duane W. Roller's Brill's New Jacoby entry on Megasthenes is paywalled and was not consulted directly.
stops.campa: The four books are lost entire, and for two thousand years nearly everything Europe believed about India came out of them. Diodorus adapts them; Strabo attacks them in one book and quotes them at length in another; Pliny the Elder turns them into data; Arrian rebuilds them into a connected account; Athenaeus, Clement, Aelian and Solinus keep single sentences. Schwanbeck gathers the pieces at Bonn in 1846 and McCrindle puts them into English at Calcutta in 1877. What is read today is a book assembled entirely out of the quotations of men who did not believe it.
suggested_refs: E. A. Schwanbeck, Megasthenis Indica: Fragmenta collegit (Bonn, 1846); J. W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian (Calcutta, 1877); Richard Stoneman, Megasthenes' Indica (Routledge, 2022)
sources: Strabo, Geography 2.1.9 and 15.1; Pliny, Natural History 6-7; Arrian, Indika; Athenaeus 4.153; Clement, Stromateis 1.15
Sir William Jones' 1793 identification of Sandracottus with Chandragupta Maurya, which made this material the anchor of ancient Indian chronology
